issues.detail: Both examples are high-level action lists with prose outputs rather than runnable demonstrations, and the auto-update example has no config or code (no electron-builder publish block, no electron-updater setup, no latest.yml snippet), so only the minimal skeleton gives concrete code.

scenarios.name: secure-ipc-file-open-bridge
scenarios.rationale: B uses event.senderFrame.origin for the sender check, as the rubric requires, and exposes a small named API with defaults left on. A checks senderFrame.url with startsWith, which is the exact thing the rubric rules out, though its other security elements are sound.

scenarios.name: harden-electron-window-navigation
scenarios.rationale: Both responses cover will-navigate, setWindowOpenHandler returning deny, CSP, an openExternal warning, and @electron/fuses with runAsNode and nodeCliInspect; A is more thorough but registers will-navigate via a broader guard and gives a CSP with default-src 'none' rather than the rubric's example, while B uses the rubric's exact CSP and is concise but has a narrower will-navigate check and less depth.

scenarios.name: github-releases-staged-autoupdate
scenarios.rationale: B covers all three rubric items with correct, specific detail (stagingPercentage added to every manifest via a script with a raising workflow, plus a Linux breakdown), though it never states outright that Electron's built-in autoUpdater doesn't work on Linux. A covers the same ground more thinly, but it does state that point explicitly. A's main weaknesses are that it only edits latest.yml by hand, says nothing about the updater needing a published (non-draft) release, and hedges on whether staging works for Linux metadata.
